description_full: Ambarella, Inc. develops low-power system-on-a-chip, semiconductors, and software for edge and physical artificial intelligence, applications, and intelligent automation. The company's system-on-a-chip (SOC) integrates third generation CVflow technology with advanced video processing, image signal processing, audio processing, and system control functions on a single chip. It also offers central domain controllers, CVflow SoCs, AI neural processors, vision processor SoCs, high-definition radars, and serializer/deserializers, as well as licenses software modules. The company's solutions are used in automotive video recorders, electronic mirrors, front advanced driver assistance system camera, AI Telematics Systems, and cabin monitoring system and driver monitoring system cameras in automotive field; central domain controllers for autonomous vehicles in autonomy; enterprise and public class, and home security cameras in the field of IoT; and enterprise, home, public spaces, and consumer applications, as well as for video conferencing, access control, healthcare, medical, and virtual reality applications. It sells its solutions to original design manufacturers, original equipment manufacturers, automotive market, and Tier-1 suppliers through its direct sales force and distributors. The company operates in Taiwan, rest of the Asia Pacific, Europe, the United States, and rest of North America. The company has a strategic collaboration with Sigma Connectivity to accelerate the development and industrialization of computer vision and edge AI products. Ambarella, Inc. was incorporated in 2004 and is headquartered in Santa Clara, California.

financial_summary: Ambarella, Inc. is a small-cap technology business with a $1.6B market cap on $391M of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +5% over the past three years and +2% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory. Operating margins are contracting by -2.9pp, the first warning that competitive pressure is eroding the franchise.
Returns on capital run at -28% against a 12% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests. Gross margins of 62% confirm genuine pricing power.
The business throws off $58M in free cash flow — roughly 15 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders.
On the balance sheet, interest coverage of 40× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield is only 0.1%, a thin return of capital, and stock-based comp at 25% of revenue is silent dilution an owner has to account for, and insiders hold 4.3% of the shares, and profit capture is only 0.0× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.
